tldr: We propose a teleoperation-free framework that builds an action-conditioned video world model using synthetic simulator data and a handful of autonomous real-robot rollouts, enabling dramatic policy improvements for whole-body humanoids via closed-loop reinforcement learning.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of WEVO. Synthetic task demonstrations and play data are generated from the LEGS simulator and combined with autonomous real robot rollouts from an initial policy to adapt a video world model (WM). A closed-loop RL environment connecting the WM, whole-body controller (WBC), VLA, and a progress reward model enables safe and efficient policy optimization.
overview:
Teaching humanoid robots whole-body loco-manipulation—coordinating locomotion and dual-arm manipulation at the same time—is one of the grand challenges in robotics. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models directly linking images, language, and actions have recently gained significant attention. However, collecting human teleoperation data on high-DoF humanoids is notoriously difficult.

While generating synthetic data in simulators is an attractive alternative, residual sim-to-real gaps in visual appearance and contact dynamics inevitably remain. Attempting to bridge this gap via direct real-world reinforcement learning (RL) poses prohibitive safety risks, such as robot falls or severe collisions with the environment.

To address this challenge, this paper introduces WEVO. The core idea lies in dividing the labor between the simulator and an action-conditioned video world model (WM). The simulator is utilized for free exploration and generating diverse "play data" (unstructured, playful interactions) to build a foundation for contact dynamics and viewpoint changes. Then, the video world model is aligned with real-world observations using just 20 autonomous real robot rollouts collected by an initial policy. Inside this realistic video world model, the robot can safely explore through hundreds of trial-and-error episodes using RL.

Across three challenging tasks evaluated on a physical humanoid robot (Unitree G1), WEVO achieved an average success rate of 75.0%, significantly outperforming baseline imitation learning (23.3%) and direct real-robot RL (48.3%). It establishes a safe and scalable new standard for humanoid training by synergistically combining the strengths of physics simulation and generative world models.
contributions: Built the first world model reinforcement learning (WM-RL) system for whole-body humanoid loco-manipulation, extending beyond fixed-base arm manipulation.
Proposed an autonomous whole-body play data collection method in simulation to teach the world model contact-rich physical dynamics and drastic viewpoint shifts during locomotion.
Established a teleoperation-free self-improvement flywheel that integrates physics simulation, 20 autonomous real robot rollouts, and closed-loop RL inside an action-conditioned video world model.
Demonstrated on real hardware that WEVO boosts mean success rates from 23.3% to 75.0%, substantially outperforming both direct real-robot RL and in-simulator RL.

sections.heading: Why Do Humanoids Need an Action-Conditioned Video World Model?
sections.summary: Humanoid whole-body manipulation makes teleoperation extremely difficult, while on-hardware RL is unsafe. This paper presents WEVO, a teleoperation-free framework that builds an action-conditioned video world model from simulation and minimal autonomous real rollouts to safely post-train policies.
sections.details:
Coordinating high-degree-of-freedom humanoid bodies makes collecting large volumes of high-quality data through human teleoperation nearly impractical. Synthetic demonstration generation in simulation environments built with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) can initialize policies automatically. However, residual gaps in visual appearance and contact dynamics persist, making real-world fine-tuning essential.

Yet, running RL directly on real hardware carries the constant risk of falling, motor burnout, or damaging the surroundings. On the other hand, existing world model reinforcement learning (WM-RL) methods have remained largely confined to tabletop tasks with fixed-base robot arms, relying heavily on human teleoperation demonstrations.

WEVO resolves this by leveraging the complementary strengths of simulation and video world models. Simulators offer safe and unlimited physical exploration, but policies trained via RL inside simulators often exploit rendering artifacts and subtle sim-to-real gaps. To solve this, the video world model—pre-trained on physical foundations in simulation—is aligned with deployment observations using only a handful of autonomous real-robot rollouts. This builds a safe, deployment-aligned virtual environment where the policy can continuously improve in a closed-loop self-training cycle.

captions.F2: Comparison of learning paradigms between prior work and WEVO. (a) Real-robot RL suffers from damage risks and low sample efficiency, while (b) conventional world model RL is limited to fixed bases and relies on teleoperation. (c) WEVO combines synthetic demonstrations, play data, and autonomous real rollouts to optimize a whole-body humanoid safely without teleoperation.

sections.heading: The Four Foundational Pillars Powering WEVO
sections.summary: The system brings together four key components: a high-fidelity simulator that reconstructs real environments, a dense progress reward model, a video world model capturing whole-body dynamics, and an RL algorithm suited for flow-matching policies.
sections.details:
WEVO carefully integrates several cutting-edge foundational technologies.

### High-Fidelity Simulator: LEGS
A real-to-sim framework that accurately reconstructs physical workspaces using 3DGS, places interactive object meshes using SAM 3D, and solves contact dynamics with MuJoCo. By integrating the SONIC whole-body controller (WBC), it can generate scripted synthetic demonstrations and exploratory behaviors without any human teleoperation.

### Dense Progress Reward Model: SARM
Training long-horizon tasks via RL requires a dense reward signal indicating how far the task has progressed. SARM hierarchically estimates task completion phases and fine-grained progress from DINOv3 vision backbone features, producing a smooth scalar reward between 0 and 1.

### Whole-Body Video World Model: DreamDojo
A generative AI model that takes the robot's current RGB frame and a sequence of commanded joint angles to predict future camera frames. Built on Cosmos, it generates egocentric video rollouts conditioned on 43-DoF humanoid joint state trajectories.

### Reinforcement Learning for Flow-Matching Policies
Modern state-of-the-art VLAs adopt flow-matching action heads. Because calculating exact action log-probabilities is challenging, this study considers three candidates: DICE-RL (optimizing an action residual on top of candidate actions), AWR (advantage-weighted regression), and ReinFlow (converting continuous flows into stochastic differential equations for PPO optimization).

sections.heading: How WEVO Trains World Models and Policies with Zero Teleoperation
sections.summary: A base policy and physical dynamics priors (play data) are trained in simulation, and the world model is aligned using 20 autonomous real rollouts. Finally, closed-loop RL with dense progress rewards is run entirely inside the world model.
sections.details:
WEVO's pipeline is carefully staged from data preparation to closed-loop learning.

### III-A: Base Policy Initialization and Autonomous Real Rollouts
First, 200 synthetic demonstrations are generated in the LEGS simulator within just 30 minutes by randomizing object locations, robot poses, and camera angles. A GR00T VLA is fine-tuned on this data to form an initial base policy. The robot runs this initial policy autonomously in the real environment to collect 20 trajectories (10 successes and 10 failures), completely free of human teleoperation or intervention.

### III-B: Two-Stage World Model Fine-Tuning
The pre-trained DreamDojo video model undergoes two-stage adaptation:
- **Intermediate Pre-training with Play Data**: 11 hours of simulated play data are collected across 100+ household objects—10 hours of manipulation with intentional grasp offsets to induce contacts and slips, and 1 hour of locomotion featuring rapid viewpoint rotations and base translations. This drastically enhances the model's prediction of contact dynamics and camera movements.
- **Task-Specific Fine-Tuning**: The model is trained on a mixture of the 200 synthetic demos and the 20 real trajectories (both successes and failures) to ground deployment-specific visual appearances (textures and lighting) into the world model.

### III-C: Closed-Loop Simulation Inside the World Model
The VLA policy, the whole-body controller (SONIC inside MuJoCo), and the video world model are connected in a loop. The VLA predicts 20 Hz task-space targets (end-effector poses, gripper state, base velocity, and base height) from image observations. SONIC-MuJoCo converts these targets into 50 Hz joint angles. Because the world model operates at 10 fps, a subsampling step $\rho=2$ is applied to align state displacement scales, generating smooth egocentric video chunks in 12-frame increments that are fed back into the VLA.

### III-D & III-E: Dense Progress Rewards and Policy RL
For each generated video frame, the trained SARM model predicts progress $p_t$. Its step-wise increase, smoothed with exponential filtering ($\alpha=0.7$), serves as the per-step dense reward. WEVO adopts DICE-RL, freezing the base VLA and training a lightweight residual action policy for stable updates. Over 15 iterative rounds, the policy generates and learns from 480 new trajectories rollouts inside the world model.

captions.F4: Dense progress prediction on a world model video rollout. As the robot picks an object from the table, turns around, and places it into a basket, the SARM model outputs a smooth, monotonic progress signal (0.0 to 1.0). The step-by-step progress delta is provided as an immediate reward to the policy.

sections.heading: Real-Robot Humanoid Experiments: Crushing Direct Sim RL
sections.summary: WEVO was evaluated on a physical Unitree G1 across three loco-manipulation tasks. Play data significantly boosted the world model's predictive accuracy, and RL inside the world model achieved a 75.0% success rate, dramatically outperforming real-robot RL and simulator RL.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted on a physical Unitree G1 across three complex tasks: "Pick-and-Place (PNP)" (walking to pick a bottle and placing it upright in a box), "Pick-Turn-Place (PTP)" (picking, turning 90 degrees, approaching, squatting, and placing into a floor basket), and "Bimanual Move Basket (Basket)" (walking to a stand, lifting a basket with both arms, carrying it to a table, and setting it down).

### Q1: Impact of Play Data on the World Model
Intermediate pre-training on play data improved all evaluation metrics across every task. In particular, interaction-region PSNR (iPSNR), which focuses on the end-effector and target object, improved by an average of 1.17 dB (surpassing the 0.93 dB gain in global PSNR), verifying substantial gains in contact dynamics fidelity. Downstream policy success trained with this world model jumped from 63.3% to 75.0%.

### Q2: World Model RL vs. Simulator RL vs. Real-Robot RL
Surprisingly, RL performed directly inside the LEGS simulator ("Sim RL") performed worse than the initial behavioral cloning baseline (BC: 23.3%), dropping to 18.3% average success. Policies trained in simulation overfitted to rendering artifacts and minor sim-to-real gaps, leading to severe deployment failures.
Meanwhile, direct RL on the real robot using only the 20 real trajectories ("Real RL") reached 48.3%. In contrast, WEVO (DICE-RL)—which built a world model from those same 20 trajectories and explored 480 virtual rollouts—achieved an impressive 75.0% success rate. This delivers more than 1.5x the performance of real-robot RL without putting physical hardware at risk.

### Q3: How to Learn from the World Model
Compared to filtering for successful trajectories like VLAW (33.3%) or using sparse rewards like WMPO (40.0%), DICE-RL (75.0%) excelled by utilizing the full rollout distribution (including failures) alongside dense progress rewards. Furthermore, an Offline setting that omitted online re-rollouts under the updated policy dropped to 58.3%, demonstrating the necessity of tracking policy distribution shifts.

captions.F5: Reinforcement learning progress across 15 rounds on three tasks. Real robot success (green) closely tracks world model training progress (blue), steadily climbing upward. In contrast, in-simulator learning (orange) plateaus or crashes, clearly illustrating the advantage of the video world model.
captions.F1: The three real-robot evaluation tasks (Pick-and-Place, Pick-Turn-Place, and Bimanual Move Basket) along with success rate comparisons. WEVO (Ours) achieves substantially higher success rates across all tasks compared to Base BC and Real RL.

sections.heading: Summary and What Lies Ahead
sections.summary: WEVO establishes a teleoperation-free self-improvement framework for whole-body humanoids by combining the physical coverage of physics simulation with the visual fidelity of a real-aligned video world model. Boosting the real-robot success rate from 23.3% to 75.0% offers key insights for future robot foundation models.
sections.details:
The most significant takeaway of this work is demonstrating the effectiveness of clear division of labor: rather than running RL directly inside a physics simulator, the simulator should provide physical interaction priors (play data) and base demonstrations, while policy optimization is conducted inside a video world model adapted to the real environment.

This architecture establishes a safe, sample-efficient reinforcement learning loop that avoids hardware damage while steering clear of simulation visual exploitation.

Future directions highlighted by the authors include general cross-embodiment transfer beyond Unitree G1-specific interfaces, long-horizon multi-camera viewpoint prediction, reducing video generation computational overhead, and fully joint adaptation between the world model and the policy.

takeaways: Running RL directly in physics simulators often fails by exploiting visual sim-to-real gaps, whereas RL inside a video world model aligned with 20 real rollouts enables deployment-grounded exploration.
Injecting unstructured "play data" (failed contacts and locomotion viewpoint shifts) into world model intermediate pre-training substantially improves physical interaction fidelity (iPSNR).
The entire improvement flywheel functions without expensive teleoperation rigs or human intervention, driven purely by synthetic simulation data and autonomous rollouts.
Successful world model RL requires three critical pillars: utilizing the full trajectory distribution (including failures), dense progress rewards, and online re-rollouts under the evolving policy.
limitations: The framework is tailored to the Unitree G1 and its SONIC controller interface, precluding zero-shot transfer to other humanoid embodiments.
Video generation inference is computationally demanding, accounting for roughly 75% of the total training time (around 12 hours on 8x H100 GPUs).
The current pipeline relies on a single egocentric camera, leaving challenges in resolving whole-body occlusions and maintaining multi-view temporal consistency for complex long-horizon tasks.
